content.title: About
content.content: An alcoholic coffee drink combines aromatic coffee with a spirit such as whiskey, rum, or brandy. It can be served hot or cold, often with cream, sugar, or spices, and is popular both in bars and home preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first known recipe for an alcoholic coffee appeared in Europe in the 17th century.
In Italy, the popular "caffè corretto" is espresso with a splash of grappa.
In the United States during the 1930s, Irish coffee (coffee with Irish whiskey and cream) became a post‑war staple.
Some recipes use flavored liqueurs such as amaretto or Kahlúa for extra taste.
Alcoholic coffee is often served in special glassware to highlight its color and aroma.

items.title: Stimulation and relaxation
items.content: Caffeine boosts alertness while moderate alcohol can promote relaxation, creating a unique balance.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols, and certain spirits (e.g., brandy) contain phenolic compounds that may act as antioxidants.

items.title: Warmth in cold weather
items.content: A hot alcoholic coffee helps warm the body and improves circulation in chilly conditions.

items.title: Caffeine‑alcohol interaction
items.content: The combination can mask the feeling of intoxication, increasing the risk of over‑consumption.

items.title: Blood pressure increase
items.content: Caffeine may temporarily raise blood pressure, and alcohol in larger amounts can amplify this effect.

items.title: Caffeine intolerance
items.content: People sensitive to caffeine should limit their intake of the drink.

content.title: How to Make
content.content: Brew a strong fresh coffee (espresso or filtered). Add 30‑50 ml of your chosen spirit, sweeten to taste (sugar, honey, or syrup), and stir. Optionally top with whipped cream, cinnamon, or grated chocolate. Serve hot or chill and serve over ice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The drink is prepared just before serving, so it does not require storage. Keep spirits in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dark place, and store ground coffee in an airtight container protected from moisture and light.

content.title: About
content.content: Cinnamon bread is a fragrant sweet loaf that incorporates ground cinnamon into the dough, often with added sugar or honey. It has a soft, slightly moist crumb and a warm spicy aroma that makes it popular as a breakfast item or a dessert.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cinnamon is one of the oldest spices, used for more than 4,000 years.
Traditional cinnamon bread is especially popular in Scandinavian and North American cultures during holiday seasons.
The combination of sweet dough and spicy cinnamon enhances satiety and lifts mood.
Some recipes replace sugar with molasses or maple syrup for a deeper caramel flavor.
Cinnamon’s essential oils release a lasting aroma during baking that can persist for several days.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Cinnamon is rich in polyphenols that help combat free radicals in the body.

items.title: Supports blood sugar regulation
items.content: Some studies suggest cinnamon may improve insulin sensitivity and reduce post‑meal glucose spikes.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory effect
items.content: Cinnamon’s essential oils have anti‑inflammatory activity, which can be beneficial in chronic inflammation.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The bread provides quick‑release carbohydrates, while cinnamon adds small amounts of minerals such as manganese and iron.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Cinnamon stimulates gastric secretions, helping with better digestion of the meal.

items.title: Cinnamon allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cinnamon, including skin itching or swelling.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet versions of cinnamon bread can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries with frequent consumption.

items.title: Glucose load
items.content: People with diabetes should monitor portion size, as the bread can quickly raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Coumarin in cinnamon
items.content: Large amounts of cinnamon (especially Cassia) contain coumarin, which can be harmful to the liver in high doses.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy cinnamon bread warm, spread with butter, honey, or jam. It pairs well with coffee or tea. Thin slices work great for toast, and the loaf can be used as a base for sweet canapés.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bread in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a freezer‑safe bag and reheat in the oven or toaster before serving.

bread-multigrain-reduced-calorie-and-or-.title: Multigrain Bread, Reduced Calorie and/or High Fiber

content.title: About
content.content: Multigrain bread with reduced calories and high fiber is made from a blend of whole grains, bran, and seeds. It has a dense texture, a light nutty aroma, and is suitable for diet-conscious eating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bread contains at least five different grain types, boosting its nutritional profile.
Calorie reduction is achieved by using high‑fiber whole‑grain flour and limiting added sugars and fats.
Fiber slows carbohydrate absorption, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.
Athletes often use this bread for post‑workout recovery due to its balanced macronutrients.
Gluten‑free versions are available by substituting wheat with alternative grains.

items.title: High Fiber Content
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate cholesterol levels.

items.title: Reduced Calorie Count
items.content: Lower calories make the bread suitable for weight‑management diets without sacrificing volume.

items.title: Rich in B‑Vitamins
items.content: The grain blend provides thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: Magnesium and Iron
items.content: These minerals are important for muscle function and oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Low Glycemic Index
items.content: Compared with white bread, it has a lower GI, aiding blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Grain Allergies
items.content: People allergic to wheat or other grains may experience reactions.

items.title: Gluten Content
items.content: The standard version contains gluten and is not suitable for celiac disease.

items.title: Excessive Fiber Intake
items.content: Too much fiber can cause bloating and gastrointestinal discomfort.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the bread as a base for sandwiches, toast, serve with avocado or low‑fat cheese, or as a side to soups. For extra flavor, toast slices until golden.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bread in an airtight bag at room temperature for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in a sealed bag for up to 3 months. Thaw at room temperature before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg white is the clear liquid surrounding the yolk. It is rich in protein, virtually free of fat and carbohydrates, and contains small amounts of B‑vitamins and minerals such as selenium and potassium. Egg white is commonly used to make omelets, scrambled eggs, or fried whites without yolk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: One large egg white provides about 3.6 g of protein and less than 0.1 g of fat.
Egg white stabilizes foams, which is why it is used in meringues and soufflés.
In cooking, the white is often separated from the yolk to reduce the calorie content of dishes.
Selenium in egg white supports antioxidant protection in the body.
Egg white is also used in cosmetics as a moisturizing and tightening ingredient.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Egg white supplies all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Practically fat‑free, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Rich in selenium
items.content: Selenium aids thyroid function and immune health.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: One egg white contains about 17 kcal, helpful for weight management.

items.title: Skin‑supporting properties
items.content: Egg white is used in facial masks to firm skin and reduce the appearance of fine lines.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Biotin binding
items.content: Raw egg whites contain avidin, which binds biotin and can lead to deficiency if consumed in excess.

items.title: Salmonella contamination
items.content: Improperly handled raw whites can harbor salmonella; cooking until fully set is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Whisk the white and cook it as an omelet, scramble it with a splash of milk or water, or fry it in a lightly oiled pan. Season with salt and herbs for an omelet, add vegetables for a scramble, or serve plain fried whites.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh eggs refrigerated at 1‑4 °C. Separated egg whites are best used within 2‑3 days, or can be frozen for up to 6 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Meatless lasagna is a layered Italian dish made with pasta sheets, tomato sauce, plant‑based mince, cheese and spices. It contains no animal protein but retains the classic taste and aroma of traditional lasagna.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetarian lasagna often replaces meat with soy mince, mushrooms or lentils, boosting plant protein content.
The classic lasagna recipe originated in the Mediterranean in the 19th century; vegetarian versions appeared in the 1970s with the rise of plant‑based cuisine.
Pasta sheets can be made from whole‑grain flour, increasing fiber levels.
Cheese is sometimes swapped for vegan alternatives made from nuts or soy protein.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Soy mince, lentils or mushrooms provide complete amino acids for muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta and vegetable additions support digestion and blood‑sugar stability.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Absence of meat and use of plant oils make the dish heart‑friendly.

items.title: Abundant vitamins and minerals
items.content: Tomatoes, spinach and other veggies supply vitamin C, potassium, iron and folate.

items.title: Supports gut health
items.content: Fiber and prebiotics from vegetables promote beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Soy‑based mince can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces and vegan cheeses often contain high salt levels; check labels.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten; use gluten‑free alternatives for celiac disease.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Boil pasta sheets until al dente, prepare a sauce with tomatoes, plant mince, onion, garlic and spices. In a baking dish layer pasta, sauce, vegan cheese, repeat. Bake at 180 °C for 30‑35 minutes until golden. Let rest 10 minutes before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked lasagna in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Freeze individual portions for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Meatless Lo Mein is a ready‑to‑cook package of wheat‑based noodles, vegetables and aromatic spices, designed for vegetarians and vegans. It is served as stir‑fried noodles with a savory sauce that mimics the classic Chinese dish, but without any meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lo Mein is a staple of Chinese cuisine, and the vegetarian version appeared in the 1970s in response to growing demand for plant‑based alternatives.
The noodles are produced by extrusion, giving them a firm bite and reducing the tendency to stick together.
The dried vegetable mix often includes carrot, cabbage, onion and mushrooms, providing bright colour and crunch after cooking.
Thanks to soy sauce and umami‑rich ingredients, meatless Lo Mein retains the deep flavour typical of the traditional dish.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Wheat noodles contain little saturated fat, making the dish more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetable additions (carrot, cabbage) boost fiber content, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Plant‑based protein
items.content: Soy sauce and optional tofu provide a modest amount of complete protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat noodles and vegetables supply B1, B2 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low sugar
items.content: The product contains no added sugars, suitable for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Soy sauce allergy
items.content: Soy sauce can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with soy allergy.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate content
items.content: Some sauce variants contain added MSG, which may cause sensitivity in certain people.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Wheat noodles have a high glycemic index, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Soy sauce adds significant sodium; low‑sodium versions are recommended for salt‑restricted diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat a small amount of vegetable oil in a pan, add the noodles and stir‑fry for 2‑3 minutes. Then add the vegetable mix and sauce, continue cooking until the vegetables are tender, about 5‑7 minutes. Optional additions include tofu, bean sprouts or fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry package in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. Once opened, use within 3‑4 months. Cooked Lo Mein should be refrigerated and consumed within 2 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato fries are thin strips of sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) that are fried or baked until golden and crispy. Sweet potatoes are grown in warm climates worldwide and have a naturally sweet, slightly nutty flavor and bright orange flesh.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potatoes are richer in beta‑carotene than regular potatoes, giving them their vivid orange color.
They belong to the morning‑glory family, not the nightshade family like regular potatoes.
In Japan, sweet potato fries are often served with a light drizzle of soy sauce and sea salt.
Sweet potatoes can thrive in poorer soils and require less water than regular potatoes.
In many cultures, sweet potatoes are a traditional dish for holidays and celebrations.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A in the body, supporting vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact when baked
items.content: When cooked properly (not over‑fried), sweet potatoes have a lower glycemic index than regular potatoes.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium supports heart function, muscle contraction, and nerve signaling.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Antioxidants such as vitamin C and anthocyanins protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High carbohydrate content
items.content: Sweet potatoes contain more carbs than many other vegetables, so portion control is important for those monitoring blood sugar.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may have an allergic reaction to sweet potatoes.

items.title: Over‑frying
items.content: Over‑cooking can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve sweet potato fries hot as a side dish or snack. Season with salt, paprika, garlic powder, or herbs. They pair well with dips such as yogurt sauce, garlic aioli, chili mayo, or guacamole.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked fries in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or air fryer to restore crispness.
